title: A10 | Organizing an Attack in Singles: Move Your Opponent First
content:
A10 · In-Game Application · Approx. 35 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Being able to identify which shot creates an opening and knowing when to accelerate.

Recommended to Learn First A09 Backcourt Smash, Frontcourt Net Shot

Technique and Decision-Making

Start by hitting deep shots to force your opponent to turn or step back, and watch to see if there’s a pause as they return to their position. If the return is short and you’re already in position, accelerate with a straight shot or aim for an open space. If your opponent still returns the shot quickly, keep hitting deep and wait for a second opportunity; avoid forcing a shot along the sideline when you’re off-balance.

Court Practice

  1. Play 10 set rounds. On the first shot, hit the shuttlecock deep; on the second shot, watch your opponent’s recovery. Only when they’ve regained their footing and the shuttlecock is high enough should you actively drive it down.
  2. Qualification Criteria Be able to identify at least three opportunities to accelerate and your opponent's position after each rally.

Common Mistakes and Corrections

If you treat the smash as a fixed first shot, it’s easy to overlook your opponent’s position. When practicing, always leave room for the rally to continue.

Self-Assessment

Your opponent has retreated to the backcourt, and the return is both deep and high—what should you do first?

First, move into a stable hitting position; once you’re firmly planted, decide whether to hit a drop shot or a smash. If you haven’t quite reached the right position, prioritize giving yourself time to recover.

Advanced Practice

After your partner returns each shot, have them tell you which shot made it hardest for them to get back into position. Compare your prediction with their answer. In the next round, adjust only the depth of the first shot, and observe whether the timing of the opening changes.

How to Return a Shot
Course Overview

title: B07 | High Forehand Serve in Singles
content:
B07 · Beginner · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

The ability to return a high serve to the backcourt in the diagonal service box.

Recommended to Learn First B05 Backhand Drop Shot

Technique and Decision-Making

Hold the racket loosely, maintain a steady grip and consistent rhythm, and hit the shuttlecock high along the diagonal. Start by aiming for a slightly wider landing zone; once you’ve established a consistent swing, gradually adjust the landing point to a narrower area. For official matches, follow the applicable competition rules regarding the serve.

Court Practice

  1. Serve 10 shuttles from each side. Aim for a specific area at the back of the court, and keep track of shots that are too short, go out of bounds, or land in the target area.
  2. Qualification Criteria Land at least 6 shots on each side within the designated area, and be in position before your opponent returns the serve after serving.

Common Mistakes and Corrections

If you’re applying more and more power but the shuttlecock isn’t going high, check your racket face and the direction of your stroke. Start by practicing with a slow swing to aim for the correct landing spot.

Self-Assessment

If one serve goes deep but the next one often goes out of bounds, which aspect should you work on first?

First, establish your stance, grip, and swing rhythm, then gradually adjust the power of your shots.

Advanced Practice

In the second round, have your partner stand on the opposite side as the receiver and observe whether you’re still watching the landing spot after serving. If you haven’t returned to your ready position by the time your opponent hits the shuttlecock, reduce the power of your next serve, aim for a specific landing zone, and then adjust your positioning.

Back to the Basics
Course Overview

title: A02 | Smash Landing Points and the Second Shot
content:
A02 · Advanced · Approx. 30 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

The ability to choose where to place the shuttlecock based on defensive positioning, and to be ready to return the next shot immediately after hitting it.

Recommended to Learn First A01 Introduction to the Smash

Technique and Decision-Making

Before making contact with the shuttlecock in the air, use your peripheral vision to check where your opponent is positioned. If your opponent is positioned toward the sideline, test the side landing zone while leaving ample space within the court; if your opponent raises their racket high, use the downward smash as the first step to create a short return. Immediately after hitting the first shot, return to a ready stance, then decide whether to move to the net or return to the center based on the opponent’s response.

Court Practice

  1. Start with 6 shots each of half-speed smashes down the line and to the backhand side. Then do 8 sets of double shots: hit the first shot with a downward angle, and feed the second shot randomly to the front court.
  2. Qualification Criteria Out of 8 sets, complete at least 5 sets of smashes, returns, and second-shuttle returns.

Common Mistakes and Corrections

If you spend too long watching where the smash lands, you’ll end up making the next shot an easy one for your opponent. First, slow down your speed to a level where you can return the shot consistently.

Self-Assessment

When your partner is standing in a straight line with their racket raised in front of them, what are the consequences of simply applying more power to that shot?

Your opponent may use your power to block the shot, and if you hit it too hard, it will be harder to return the second shot. Try aiming for a shot that lands close to your opponent or a more controlled drop shot.

Advanced Practice

In the second round, have the feeder randomly return to the left or right side of the net after you hit a smash, and note the direction of each move. If your placement is on target but you frequently fail to get to the second shot in time, reduce the smash speed by one level for the next set and compare the results again.

How to Return a Shot
Course Overview

title: A08 | Two-Shot Placement for the Flat Drive Fast Attack
content:
A08 · Advanced · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Use the first shot to restrict your opponent's swing, then change the direction of the second shot.

Recommended to Learn First A07 Introduction to the Flat Drive

Technique and Decision-Making

On your first shot, aim slightly outside your opponent’s comfort zone and watch to see if the racket head is forced toward their body; on your second shot, wait until you see an opening before changing direction. If your opponent is still able to hit the shuttlecock early in front of them, return a steady shot down the middle first to preserve the opportunity to change direction on your next shot.

Court Practice

  1. Half-court doubles flat drive. On the first shot, aim for the side of your body; on the second shot, aim for the outside based on your partner’s position. After completing 8 sets of double shots, allow free choice.
  2. Qualification Criteria Out of 8 shots, at least 5 should have distinguishable landing points on both sides of the net, and the racket should not be pulled back significantly to adjust the trajectory.

Common Mistakes and Corrections

If you pull your arm back too far before each stroke, you’ll be a split second too slow. Use an empty racket to check whether the racket head remains in front of your body at all times.

Self-Assessment

If your opponent remains firmly on the outside after the first shot, do you have to hit to the outside on the second shot according to the practice sequence?

No need. If there’s no opening on the outside, choose the safer middle or the side of your body, and wait until the next shot to change the direction.

Advanced Practice

To increase the difficulty, have your partner return the shuttlecock with a flat drive first, then choose where to place your second shot. For each set, record only three outcomes: “inside, center, or outside.” This helps you determine whether you’re changing direction because you spotted an opening or because you made the decision in advance.

How to Return a Shot
Course Overview

title: A04 | Net Play Decision-Making: Dive for the Shuttlecock or Drop Shot
content:
A04 · Advanced · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

The ability to choose between a smash and a drop shot based on the height of the shot and balance.

Recommended to Learn First A03 Introduction to Net Dives

Technique and Decision-Making

Use a slight downward stroke only when the incoming shot is high and still within your striking range. If the shot is low and you’re sliding forward, first guide the racket gently over the net. For both types of shots, lead with the racket head toward the shuttlecock and make your final adjustment just before contact to avoid revealing your choice too early.

Court Practice

  1. A partner serves a total of 12 net shots—a mix of high and low shots. First, verbally call out “dive” or “drop” before swinging the racket. In the second round, omit the verbal cue.
  2. Qualification Criteria It’s reasonable to aim for at least 9 shots in the final rally, while keeping your body and racket from touching the net.

Common Mistakes and Corrections

When you try to hit a low shot even lower, it’s easy to hit the net. First, use the pause function to review the relative height of the shuttlecock and the net at the moment of contact.

Self-Assessment

When the shuttlecock is served below the net and the racket head is very close to the net, which shot is the most reliable?

Prioritize using a controlled racket face for net shots or clear shots, depending on where you make contact with the shuttlecock and your opponent’s position.

Advanced Practice

After completing the stationary feeding drill, incorporate the same task into a four-stroke drill in half-court. Your partner should focus on only two things: whether you chose the correct shot, and whether you were able to maintain your balance after hitting the shuttlecock. Record the most common mistake for each item once.

How to Return a Shot
Course Overview

title: A09 | Backcourt Smash, Net Shot
content:
A09 · Advanced · Approx. 35 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Able to work with a partner to execute backcourt smashes and frontcourt blocks.

Recommended to Learn First A02 Smash Landing Points and the Second Shot

Technique and Decision-Making

From the backcourt, hit the shuttlecock downward with enough power to maintain balance; from the frontcourt, position yourself where you can block a straight shot while leaving room to turn and cover the diagonal. In the second round, let your partner freely block either a straight or diagonal shot; both players should observe the shuttlecock’s speed and height over the net before deciding who moves forward first.

Court Practice

  1. Three-person drill. Backcourt player hits a half-speed straight-line drop shot; the player on the opposite side blocks the straight-line shot first, while the frontcourt player intercepts it. The third player blocks the diagonal shot freely. Perform a total of 12 sets.
  2. Qualification Criteria In the stationary drills, players should maintain proper positioning for at least 6 repetitions; in the directional change drills, players should call out who is responsible before a shuttle is missed.

Common Mistakes and Corrections

If a front-court player stands too close to the net, they’re likely to miss a flat drive. Step back to a position where you have time to react and can still block the net, then make slight adjustments to the landing spot based on the back-court player’s position.

Self-Assessment

After a teammate hits a cross-court shot from the backcourt, should the player at the net still stand on the original straight line?

Reassess your opponent’s shot location and the likely return path; both players should move together to avoid leaving gaps in the middle.

Advanced Practice

Groups of four can take turns practicing two types of shots: the backcourt straight-line smash and the backcourt cross-court smash. After switching roles within each group, compare which shot makes it easiest for the frontcourt player to block the shuttle, and agree on a division of labor for returning cross-court shots.

Next Lesson in This Series A10 Singles Offensive Strategy: Move Your Opponent First

How to Return a Shot

title: A06 | Fast Drop Shots and Slow Drop Shots
content:
A06 · Advanced · Approx. 30 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

The time difference between a fast drop shot and a slow drop shot.

Recommended to Learn First A05 Introduction to Backcourt Lobs

Technique and Decision-Making

First, get into position, shift your weight to the side, and maintain a racket position similar to that used for a high clear. A fast drop shot sends the shuttlecock to the front court more quickly, while a slow drop shot brings it closer to the net; however, if it clears the net too high, it gives your opponent an opportunity to attack. Compare how these two shots affect your time to recover to your position; when you’re behind the shuttlecock, prioritize a safe landing spot.

Court Practice

  1. From the same backcourt spot, hit 6 fast drops and 6 slow drops, using two target zones in the front court to observe the height and landing point of the shuttlecock as it crosses the net.
  2. Qualification Criteria Hit at least 4 of each type of drop shot into the target area, and identify which shot you can execute more consistently.

Common Mistakes and Corrections

If your soft drop shots consistently go too high over the net, first stabilize your contact point, reduce the difference in swing speed, and then make gradual adjustments.

Self-Assessment

Should You Keep Practicing the Same Slow Lift Shot to the Same Spot When Your Opponent Is Already Positioned at the Net?

First, adjust your shot based on your opponent’s position—try a quick drop shot or a drive to the backcourt—and see if it disrupts their movement.

Advanced Practice

Ask your partner to call out the direction and landing spot of every shot, and return to the ready position after hitting the shuttlecock. After practicing, count how many low returns each of the fast drop shot and slow drop shot produce, then choose one of them to incorporate into the rally.

How to Return a Shot
Course Overview

title: Clear Shots and Positioning: Using Backcourt Shots to Re-establish Your Position on the Court
content:
D07 · Advanced · Approx. 30 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Use a high clear to buy time to get back into position and prepare for the next shot.

Court Practice

  1. Practice a two-shot drill combining a high clear and a net return, for a total of 8 sets. After the first shot, adjust your position before returning the second shot.
  2. Qualification Criteria In at least 5 out of 8 sets, both shots must clear the net, and a preparatory step must be taken before the second shot.

Defensive Skills / Clear Shots and Returning to Position

Practice the positioning, contact, and recovery for the forehand high clear, and use the return as a tool to adjust the pace of the rally.

A High Clear Is About More Than Just Hitting the Shuttlecock Far

A high clear sends the shuttlecock to the opponent’s backcourt and can be used to adjust the pace of the rally and buy time to move into position. This lesson starts with the forehand backcourt clear—which is easy to execute—focusing first on consistency and distance before incorporating movement. Whether a high clear is appropriate depends on the incoming shot, your opponent’s position, and your own abilities; you shouldn’t treat every return as the same situation.

Key Points for Preparation and shuttle Contact

Move early to a position where you can control the shot, preparing with a relaxed grip and fluid body movements. This makes it easier to consistently hit the shuttle in the same spot and avoids having to scramble to make a full-force recovery once the shuttlecock is already behind you. After completing your swing, regain your balance and prepare your grip; don’t just focus on how far the shuttlecock flies and neglect whether you’ll be ready for the next shot.

Illustrative diagrams of lesson scenarios; for details on techniques, please refer to the BWF instructional materials below and follow the on-site guidance.

Drills for Transitioning from Stationary to Moving Positions

Start by having a partner consistently feed you easy-to-handle high shots, aiming for a larger target area in the backcourt; then incorporate short-range positioning drills; and finally, practice moving forward and backward. Play six to eight shots per set, tracking in-bounds shots, backcourt depth, and positioning balance. Adjust the number of sets based on your physical condition; if you make repeated mistakes, lower the difficulty first—there’s no need to swing with full force on every shot to chase distance.

Common Mistakes

If you frequently fail to reach the backcourt, first check whether you’re arriving too late, gripping the racket too tightly, or your movements are disjointed. If you often hit the shuttle out of bounds, leave a safety margin and control the direction of your shots. If it takes several steps to regain your balance after a shot, return to stationary drills at a fixed position; once you can complete your follow-through, gradually increase your range of movement.

BWF Video Viewing Assignment

The "Forehand Clear" instructional material can be used as a reference for the forehand clear. First, observe the setup and point of contact, then pay attention to how the follow-through connects to the next step. The practice schedule and recording methods on this site are provided as learning aids; the videos themselves retain the original publisher’s content and copyright.

Adjust Your Position Based on the Situation

When returning to your position, don’t run to the same fixed spot for every shot. First, assess your return, your opponent’s position, and the possible shot trajectories, then adjust your stance accordingly. In doubles, coordinate with your partner to divide offensive and defensive responsibilities; in singles, stay aware of the space in both the front and back courts. You can expand this to include footwork and movement classifications, practicing shots and movement together.

After hitting a high clear, your opponent has moved to the back right corner of the court. What should you look for before deciding where to reposition yourself?

First, observe your opponent’s contact point, body balance, and the area you can cover. Move into a position where you can respond to the main shot direction, and take a preparatory step as your opponent swings.

title: Defensive Flat Drive: Handling Body Shots and Quick Forehand-Backhand Transitions
content:
D05 · Advanced · Approx. 30 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Maintaining a front-body stroke when the shuttlecock is returned alternately from both sides.

Court Practice

  1. Have a partner alternate between serving to the forehand and backhand sides, 10 shuttles per set. Start with a fixed direction, then add one random shuttle starting with the second set.
  2. Qualification Criteria In the final set of 7 shots, you should be able to consistently return the shuttlecock over the net, with the racket head returning to near your chest after each shot.

Defensive Skills / Flat Drive Defense

Start with your stance and forehand-to-backhand transitions, and practice returning shots steadily under pressure from flat shots.

Learning Objectives for This Lesson

When defending against flat drives—which involve faster flat shots and pressure on your backhand side—the key is timely preparation, maintaining balance, and making sound decisions. This lesson begins with partner drills, then incorporates simple directional changes. Consistently returning the shuttlecock to the court and being ready for the next shot builds a stronger foundation than occasionally forcing a spectacular counter-drive.

Leave Room to React First

Keep the racket in front of your body and hold it loosely, adjusting your forehand or backhand stroke based on the incoming shot. Do not let the racket hang down by your side, and avoid using the same side of the racket to block every shot. When facing shots close to your body, shorten your stroke and maintain adequate space to move; adjust your footwork when necessary, rather than simply leaning back or swinging the racket too widely.

Illustrative diagrams of lesson scenarios; for details on techniques, please refer to the BWF instructional materials below and follow the on-site guidance.

Segmented Practice

Two players hit flat shots in a fixed direction while maintaining a safe distance. Start by exchanging five shots, then alternate between forehand and backhand strokes. In the next phase, have your partner change the direction of the shot at a controlled speed, and practice identifying the shot’s trajectory before returning it. Keep each set short; take a break if the quality of play declines. Do not aim for the head or face, and avoid chasing the shuttle at full speed at close range.

Common Mistakes and Corrections

When you keep getting pinned by the shuttlecock, first check your ready position and stance—don’t just try to move faster. If you get stuck switching between forehand and backhand, slow down the pace and practice adjusting your grip and racket angle. If your returns keep floating high, recheck your point of contact and minimize unnecessary movements; avoid trying to compensate by hitting harder on every shot.

How to Use the Videos

The BWF’s “Midcourt Game with Body Hits” below is a teaching resource for midcourt groundstrokes. On this page, we use it as an aid for observing the direction of incoming shots and preparing your racket position. During actual practice, aim for a safe space; start by working together to control the shuttle’s speed, then gradually increase the pressure. The viewing tips and difficulty adjustments were written by our site.

Transitioning from Defense to Offense

When the incoming shot and your position allow it, gradually practice returning the flat shot to an open space; if conditions aren’t ideal, focus on returning the shot consistently first. During doubles practice, coordinate with your partner to divide responsibilities in the middle of the court to avoid collisions caused by both players going for the same shot. You can combine this with a lesson on flat drives for quick attacks to compare the objectives of the same technique in offensive and defensive situations.

Self-Assessment

When hitting consecutive flat drives, I can return them with my forehand, but my backhand is often a split-second too slow. How should I practice this next?

Slow down the pace of the feeds from both sides so you can make contact with the shuttlecock in front of you. After hitting each shuttlecock, first relax your fingers and bring the racket head back in front of you, then switch to the backhand side.

title: The Lift Shot for Escape: From the Backhand Lift to Gaining Time to Get Back into Position
content:
D03 · Beginner · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

When receiving a shot from the backcourt, be able to lift the shuttlecock high for a safe return.

Court Practice

  1. Start with the backhand net shot. Do 2 sets in a row, with 8 shots per set. After returning the shot, return to the designated ready position and return the next shot.
  2. Qualification Criteria Make sure at least 5 shots per set land in the backcourt, and keep your eyes on your opponent's side of the court as you return to your position.

Defensive Skills / Lob Shots for Escape

Practice hitting low shots from the front court to the back court, using height and depth to buy time to adjust your position.

The Uses and Limitations of the Lift Shot

When a shot from the front court is no longer suitable for a smash, a lift can send the shuttlecock to the back court, buying you time to get back into position. However, if the lift is too short or lacks sufficient height, it may make it easier for your opponent to attack. As a beginner, aim for the legal backcourt target zone to establish consistent shots, then gradually adjust the height, length, and direction.

Hitting the Shuttlecock in Front of You and Racket Control

Move toward the incoming shuttlecock in a balanced manner, bringing your racket to a position where you can return it in front of your body, and adjust your grip according to whether you’re using your forehand or backhand. This lesson begins with the backhand lift; avoid simply bending your wrist upward forcefully. Complete the stroke smoothly, then return to a position ready to handle the next shot—do not swing your entire body out in an attempt to hit the shuttlecock farther.

Illustrative diagrams of lesson scenarios; for details on techniques, please refer to the BWF instructional materials below and follow the on-site guidance.

Three-Stage Practice

Start by having a partner toss the shuttlecock steadily to get a feel for the point of contact between the shuttlecock and the racket face; then incorporate stepping and returning to your position; finally, have the partner vary the direction of the toss from left to right. Play eight shuttles per set, and record the number of times each shuttlecock lands in bounds and reaches the designated backcourt area. If most land in the midcourt, slow down the pace and check your timing and movement coordination.

Common Mistakes

If the shuttlecock frequently drifts toward the sideline, check the angle of your racket face and where you’re making contact with the shuttlecock; if you lose your balance as soon as you apply force, start by shortening your stride. Don’t aim right at the baseline every time—leave yourself some safety margin. Adjust the intensity of your practice so that you can maintain your movements; if you feel any discomfort, stop increasing the workload.

BWF Viewing Tips

The "Backhand Lift" is the BWF term for the backhand lift shot. You can observe the racket grip and ready position, shuttle contact control, and follow-through. This site combines video playback instructions with practice notes on the same page to help you identify what to practice after watching—and does not present the video as the only technique suitable for everyone.

Returning a Clear and Getting Back into Position

Immediately after lifting the shuttlecock, resume scanning the court to confirm whether your opponent is in position and identify the areas you need to cover. In doubles, coordinate defensive positioning with your partner after lifting the shuttlecock; in singles, adjust your positioning based on the incoming shot and your opponent’s position. For further reading, explore the classification of high clears and positioning strategies to understand the timing and effectiveness of different backcourt returns.

Your backhand lift often lands in the middle of the court—how should you determine the cause?

title: Blocking a Smash: First, stabilize the racket face, then decide whether to block the shot or return it.
content:
D01 · Beginner · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

The ability to use a steady racket face to block a controllable return to the net.

Court Practice

  1. Have a partner feed you 3 sets of 6 shots each at half speed. For each set, first designate a specific landing zone along a straight line, and record the reasons for shots going out of bounds or into the net.
  2. Qualification Criteria In the last set, hit at least 4 shots to the front court, and don't let your elbow pull back with the racket face.

Defensive Skills / Blocking Smashes at the Net

Use slower smashes to develop front-court contact and control of short movements, and gradually practice the next move after a defensive play.

Focus on Consistency in Defense

You don’t always have to hit a smash with full force. A net return can change the space your opponent has to cover, but you must also consider the shuttlecock’s speed, where you make contact, and your opponent’s position. As a beginner, start by practicing consistent returns that land back in the court. Make sure you can control the shuttlecock in front of you before adding different options like net returns, flat drives, or lifts.

Ready Position and Reaction

Keep your knees naturally bent and maintain your balance. Position your racket in front of you where you can react quickly; avoid waiting until the shuttlecock is right next to you before raising your racket. Stay relaxed in your ready position, and adjust your forehand or backhand stance based on the direction of the incoming shuttlecock. Use short, concise strokes to return the shuttlecock, and return to your ready position immediately after hitting it. Avoid using a wide swing for every smash; this will give you time to transition to your next shot.

Illustrative diagrams of lesson scenarios; for details on techniques, please refer to the BWF instructional materials below and follow the on-site guidance.

Start with Slow Shots and Fixed Directions

Have a partner feed you shots in a fixed direction at a controlled speed. Start by practicing ten shots that stay in bounds, then shift your focus to a larger area in the front court. Only increase the speed or vary the direction once you’re comfortable. The feeder and the player should maintain a safe distance. If you can no longer keep up, lower the difficulty or take a break; avoid replacing effective practice with a series of forced returns.

Common Problems and Corrections

If the shuttlecock frequently bounces too high, minimize unnecessary racket swings and regain control of the racket face; if the shuttlecock frequently goes into the net, check whether you’re making contact too late or aiming too close to the net. If you lose your balance after hitting the shuttlecock, slow down first to restore the flow between your preparation, contact, and recovery. When evaluating your progress, consider both the quality of your return and whether you’re ready for the next shot.

How to Pair Videos

The BWF Block Defense instructional material below can serve as a reference for defensive movements. When watching, first observe the ready position and racket movements before and after contact, then compare them with your own stationary drills. The practice sequence on this page is a recommendation from this site; it is not an official test or verbatim transcript of the video.

Keep Reading the Return Even After Defending

Blocking a shot doesn’t necessarily mean you have to rush the net. First, assess the quality of the return, where your opponent made contact, and your partner’s role, then decide how to move. In doubles, agree on defensive zones with your partner beforehand, and gradually practice covering each other’s positions after returning the shuttlecock to avoid both of you chasing the same shuttlecock at the same time.

title: Flat Drive Fast Attack: Apply Pressure Through Short Movements, Placement, and Continuous Preparation
content:
A07 · Advanced · Approx. 30 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Maintain the speed of a flat drive by making contact with the shuttlecock near the front of the racket and using a short swing.

Court Practice

  1. Two players stand at the halfway line and perform 4 sets of straight drives, aiming for 8 strokes per set. Starting with the third set, alternate between returning the shuttlecock to the inside and outside of the body.
  2. Qualification Criteria In at least 2 out of 4 sets, reach 8 strokes, and have the racket head back in front of your body before the next shot arrives.

Offensive Strategies / Flat Drive Quick Attack

First, establish a consistent rhythm for your flat drives, then practice hitting the shuttle into open spaces—avoid simply competing to see who can swing the racket harder.

What Is the Purpose of the Flat Drive Quick Attack?

The flat drive involves a short rally; the goal is to keep the shuttlecock on a relatively flat, straight path and gain the initiative through placement and follow-through. This lesson begins with a controllable, moderate speed. Start by returning the shuttlecock continuously, then practice targeting open spaces. Speed is just one factor; whether your opponent can return the shuttlecock comfortably and whether you’re ready for the next shot are equally important.

Grip and Short-Range Control

Keep the racket in front of you where you can react quickly. Hold the racket loosely, allowing your fingers and forearm to work together to control the racket face. The shorter the rally, the less suitable it is to make wide swings. When switching between forehand and backhand strokes, focus on adjusting your grip to get into position quickly; avoid swinging your entire arm widely on every shot, as you’ll need to recover quickly and be ready for the next shot.

Illustrative diagrams of lesson scenarios; for details on techniques, please refer to the BWF instructional materials below and follow the on-site guidance.

From Cooperation to Choice

Two players should practice flat drives in a fixed direction while maintaining a safe distance. Start by aiming for five to ten consecutive shots; once you’re comfortable, alternate between forehand and backhand strokes, then add designated open-space directions. Introduce only one variation at a time. If you make consecutive errors as soon as you pick up the pace, return to a rhythm where you can maintain quality, then gradually increase the pressure of the incoming shots.

Common Mistakes

If the shuttlecock keeps floating upward, first check your racket face and point of contact—don’t just try to compensate by hitting faster. If you frequently can’t keep up with the next shot, shorten your swing and make sure your racket returns to your front. If you’re hitting too hard and the shuttlecock often goes out of bounds, focus instead on keeping the shuttlecock in bounds and controlling its direction. Leave plenty of space in the practice area to avoid hitting the shuttlecock hard toward your partner’s head or face at close range.

BWF Video Challenges

The "Flat Play" instructional material can be used to observe the rhythm and preparation involved in flat shots. This page expands on that concept to include drills for targeting offensive landing spots: first, watch how the shuttlecock moves back and forth, then visualize where you’ll position yourself for your next shot. The video provides a demonstration, while this site organizes segmented drills and self-assessment questions.

Applying Them in Matches

During doubles practice, first agree on who will defend which area after a flat drive, then gradually incorporate moving to the net and dropping back. Even after hitting a fast shot, continue to watch your opponent’s return to avoid assuming you’ve already gained the upper hand. For further reading, check out the lesson on flat drive defense, which compares the purposes of the same type of flat shot in different situations.

During a flat drive drill, the shuttlecock gets pushed right next to my body on the third stroke. How can I keep the rally going?

Start by shortening your backswing, bringing the racket head back in front of your body, and leaving space for your elbow. Perform four consecutive strokes at a slower pace; once you’ve stabilized your form, you can increase the speed.

title: Drop Shot Practice: Use Similar Preparations to Vary the Landing Point and the Pace of the Rally
content:
A05 · Beginner · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Use a stance similar to that for a high clear to place the drop shot in the front court.

Court Practice

  1. Have a partner consistently serve 10 shuttles to the backcourt. Start by hitting only straight drop shots, then mix in 4 high clears for the last 4 shuttles.
  2. Qualification Criteria Out of 10 shots, at least 6 should land in the designated area, while maintaining a stable stance before hitting the shuttlecock.

Offensive Strategies / Drop Shot

Start with straight drop shots from a fixed position, and practice gentle control, returning to your position, and choosing between clear shots and drop shots.

Learning Objectives for the Drop Shot

A drop shot sends a shuttle from the backcourt to the opponent’s frontcourt; it can be used to change the rhythm of the rally and force the opponent to move. It’s not just a matter of reducing power—it also requires positioning yourself early and precise racket-face control. For beginners, the priority is to ensure consistent shot placement and reasonable landing points; only then should you gradually work on handling faster shots. There’s no need to aim for shots that are very close to the net right from the start.

Preparation and Shot Strategy

Start by assuming the overhead stroke stance used for returning a high clear. Make contact with the shuttlecock at a position where you can maintain control of your body, and complete the motion smoothly. Avoid lowering your arm too early or stopping your swing entirely just because you intend to drop the shuttlecock. If you’re out of position and the shuttlecock is already behind you, first choose a return that allows you to maintain your balance, then work to regain your position.

Illustrative diagrams of lesson scenarios; for details on techniques, please refer to the BWF instructional materials below and follow the on-site guidance.

Three-Part Drill

In the first set, have a partner feed you the shuttlecock steadily, focusing solely on straight drop shots; in the second set, alternate between high clears and drop shots, observing whether your preparation differs too much between them; in the third set, ask your partner to give simple instructions, and practice confirming the instructions before choosing your shot. Play eight shuttles per set, initially aiming for a larger area in the front court, then narrowing the target once you’ve stabilized your shots.

Common Mistakes

If you frequently hit the shuttlecock into the net, don’t just swing harder—first check whether you’re arriving late or making contact too low. If the shuttlecock floats too high, re-evaluate your direction and racket angle. Staying in place after a drop shot makes it easy to miss your preparation for the next shot, so you should return to your starting position after every shot. During practice, pay attention to both the quality of your stroke and your body balance.

Key Points to Watch in the Video

The BWF’s “Overhead Drop Shot” can serve as a reference for the overhead drop shot technique. Before watching, choose one of the following: the ready position, shuttle contact control, or follow-through. After watching, review the concept in slow motion, then discuss any differences with your coach or playing partner. Don’t assume that two techniques are the same just because the results look similar.

From Practice to Application

Incorporate both high clears and dropshots into your half-court rallies. Note when your opponent needs to move forward and whether you can get back into position in time. The value of an offensive shot can also lie in creating opportunities for the next shot. Combine this with smashing drills to understand how placement, speed, and preparation influence one another.

title: net kills: Judging Height, Shortening Your Movement, and Preparing for the Next Shot
content:
A03 · Beginner · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Being able to identify net shots where there is room to smash down.

Court Practice

  1. Have a partner at the net alternate between hitting 6 high shots and 4 low shots. Use a short swing to return the high shots, and let the low shots drop at the net.
  2. Qualification Criteria Correctly judge at least 8 shots, and be able to finish all net kills within your own half of the court.

Offensive Strategies / Diving for Shots at the Net

First, identify shots that can be smashed downward, then practice the forehand smash with short, concise movements to avoid hitting the net and lunging too far forward.

First, Determine Whether You Can Drive the Shuttlecock Downward

When diving for a shuttle at the net, don’t automatically hit it hard just because you see it near the net. You should only hit it downward if the shuttle’s position, the height at which you make contact, and your physical condition allow it; if the shuttle is already below the optimal position for an attack, you should instead use a net shot or a lift. Good judgment is more important than speed; avoid forcing a shot that could have extended the rally and ending up with an error.

Waiting with the Racket in Front of You

Get into your ready position early, maintain your balance as you approach the shuttlecock, and control the racket face with small movements. Since you have very little time at the net, there’s no need to swing the racket widely; after hitting the shuttlecock, be sure to bring the racket back in time to prepare for the next shot. Pay special attention to your distance from the net to avoid hitting the net with your racket or body, and don’t lunge forward to reach the shuttlecock.

Illustrative diagrams of lesson scenarios; for details on techniques, please refer to the BWF instructional materials below and follow the on-site guidance.

Start with Fixed Feeding

Have a partner stand in a safe position and feed you easy high shots near the net. Start by practicing directing the shuttlecock into open spaces, and avoid hitting the shuttlecock forcefully toward the feeder. Play six shots per set; begin by keeping your position fixed, then add lateral movements. In the next stage, mix in lower shots and challenge yourself to choose between smashing, dropping, and lifting the shuttlecock, rather than smashing every shot.

Common Mistakes

If you frequently hit the net, shorten your swing first and check where you’re making contact with the shuttlecock; if you’re hitting the shuttlecock but it’s always going out of bounds, reduce your power and widen your target area first. If you can’t get back into position after returning a shot, check whether you’re moving too quickly or taking too big a final step. First, keep your movements within a range where you can stop and recover, then increase the pace.

BWF Demonstration—How to Watch

The video below is a BWF Development instructional clip on the forehand net drop shot. Watch it while keeping three questions in mind: Where is the racket during the setup? How brief is the contact motion? How do you reset after the shot? The shuttle-feeding sequence and recording method used on this site are designed as extended practice exercises, not as a frame-by-frame, word-for-word commentary on the demonstrator’s movements.

Incorporating the Dive into Doubles Play

First, agree with your partner on who will play the front and back courts, and practice waiting at the net for the right opportunity. When you don’t have a good angle for a smash, it’s still valuable to keep the rally going with a solid return. After each set, reflect on whether your decisions were sound, and gradually develop the habit of assessing the shuttle’s height, deciding on your shot, and preparing for the next stroke.

title: A Beginner's Guide to the Smash: From the Point of Contact and Landing Spot to Preparing for the Next Shot
content:
A01 · Beginner · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

First, locate the sweet spot in the upper front part of your body, then hit the shuttlecock toward the designated area with moderate force.

Court Practice

  1. Have a partner serve you 10 high shuttles; start by aiming for straight-line targets. Each time the shuttle lands, return to your ready position before receiving the next one.
  2. Qualification Criteria Land 6 out of 10 shots in the target and maintain your balance before the next serve.

Offensive Strategies / Smash

First, practice hitting the shuttlecock downward with controlled power, then coordinate the landing spot with your return to position after the smash.

When Is the Right Time to Hit a Smash?

The purpose of the smash is to apply downward pressure, forcing a weak return or ending the rally. You should only attempt a smash when the height and position of the incoming shot, as well as your own balance, are favorable; if the shuttlecock has already landed behind you, there’s no need to force a powerful swing just to attack. In this lesson, we’ll start by practicing controlled smashes without jumping to get comfortable with the stroke and returning to your position, then gradually increase the speed.

Preparation and Key Points for Hitting the Shuttlecock

Move early to a position where you can hit the shuttlecock in front of and above you, using a relaxed forehand grip. Ensure a smooth transition between your body rotation and racket swing; avoid simply bending your wrist forcefully or gripping the racket handle too tightly. After making contact, complete the motion naturally and return to your ready position. Focus on placement and body balance rather than the sound or speed of a single shot.

Illustrative diagrams of lesson scenarios; for details on techniques, please refer to the BWF instructional materials below and follow the on-site guidance.

Phased Practice Schedule

Start by swinging the racket without a shuttlecock to check your direction, then have a partner feed you high shots that are easy to reach. In the first set, focus only on getting the shuttlecock over the net and landing it within the court; in the second set, aim for a larger, straight-line target area; and in the third set, add smashes and return to your position afterward. Play six shots per set, take a break between sets, and switch partners to observe each other. This is the beginner’s routine on this site; you can scale it back based on your fitness level—there’s no need to start with consecutive, full-power smashes right away.

Common Mistakes and Corrections

If you frequently hit the shuttlecock into the net, check whether you’re making contact too low or hitting too forcefully in an attempt to achieve a certain angle. If the shuttlecock frequently goes out of bounds, first reduce your power and refocus on your contact point. If you lose your balance after hitting a smash, return to stationary drills to ensure you’re completing your stroke properly. If you experience discomfort in your shoulders, elbows, or wrists, stop increasing the intensity and ask your coach to help assess the issue.

Video Viewing Assignment

When watching the BWF’s “The Smash” instructional videos, pay close attention to the preparatory stance, the point of contact, and the follow-through. First, identify a specific movement you want to model; pause the video and practice the swing in slow motion to get a feel for it. The text and number of practice sets on this page were designed by this site and are not a word-for-word translation of the video or the BWF’s proficiency rating standards.

Post-Class Notes

Keep track of the number of times you hit the shuttlecock in bounds, near the target, and return it to a balanced position in each set, and note the situations where you make the most mistakes. Once you’ve stabilized your form, have your partner vary the landing spots to practice deciding whether to hit a smash, a drop shot, or a clear. For further reading, check out the lesson on drop shots in the “Offensive Techniques” section to understand how to combine speed and placement.

My smash placement is on point, but I can’t seem to return the next shot in time. What should I focus on adjusting first in the next set?

Start by reducing the downward force so you can immediately retract your racket and steady your stance after hitting the shuttlecock. Have your partner feed you a steady stream of shuttlecocks, and only increase the speed once you’ve confirmed you can return to your position consistently.

title: How to Analyze Match Videos: Learn to Read Tactics Using Game Notes
content:
M05 · Beginner · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

The ability to keep track of points in a consistent manner.

Court Practice

  1. Choose a continuous match and record the duration, shot patterns, and outcomes of 8 rallies. Start by tracking only one player.
  2. Qualification Criteria Identify recurring situations and write down one drill you can practice on the court.

Choose a Full BWF Replay to Practice

Class Notes · Practice and Observations

Start with a Single Observation Question, and Turn Watching Matches into Learning Through Pauses, Replays, and Game Notes.

First, Choose an Observation Exercise

Watching an entire match is fun, but when using it for learning, start by identifying a specific question: How do players get back into position? Where do they place their racket when returning a serve? Or how do they adjust after a series of attacks? The more specific the question, the easier it is to find evidence in the replay. Don’t try to record every type of shot, score, and position at once—otherwise, you’ll end up spending all your time just taking notes.

Part 1—Watching an Entire Rally

Start by watching the video normally to understand how a rally begins and ends. Focus on the general flow—for example, if one player consistently sends the shuttlecock to the backcourt, or if a net shot forces the opponent to lift the shuttlecock. Camera angles may obscure the landing spot and other details; mark any unclear parts as “uncertain,” and avoid presenting guesses as facts.

Part 2—Three Key Moments to Pause At

Pause the action when your opponent hits the shuttlecock, when you make contact with the shuttlecock, and after the shot, to observe your ready position, body balance, the shuttlecock’s position, and your next move. The same result can stem from different causes; a mistake does not necessarily indicate a wrong choice—it may also be related to timing, the quality of your contact, or pressure from your opponent.

Part 3—Comparing Other Rounds

Find another rally in a similar situation and see if the player changes their shot placement, rhythm, or positioning. When you only have a highlight clip, it can be difficult to determine whether a particular choice is made repeatedly, so it’s helpful to refer to the full match video. Prioritize official BWF TV content as your source, and avoid drawing conclusions based solely on clips taken out of context.

Bringing Your Notes to Practice

Use three columns to record the situation, the options you observe, and the skills you can practice. For example: the opponent hits the ball to the net; the player prepares early by holding the racket; next time, practice returning to the net position after initiating the shot. This is a method for recording match observations proposed by this site; it is not an authoritative evaluation of a player’s style. Practice should still be adjusted according to your own skill level.

Common Questions When Watching a Match

Can You Just Copy What Professional Players Do? First, understand the purpose, then choose which aspects to practice based on your own ability. Are spectacular shots always the best choice? It still depends on the score, court position, and your opponent’s reaction. Start with this site’s articles on scoring and watching matches, then use official videos to practice the three-step observation method described above.

Back to Course Overview　｜　Official BWF TV Videos

Back to Match Observations
Course Overview

Self-Assessment

If You Only Focus on the Point-Winning Shot, What Information Are You Missing?

First, review the one or two shots leading up to the point. Note where your opponent was drawn out of position, the height of the shot, and their position after hitting the shuttlecock, then look for similar rallies to compare.

title: Observing the First Three Shots in Doubles: Reading the Transition from Offense to Defense Based on the Serve
content:
M02 · Advanced · Approx. 30 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

The ability to determine who gains the higher hitting position during the first three rallies.

Court Practice

  1. Select 10 serve-and-return sequences from a full doubles replay, and note the landing spot of the second shot and whether the third shot forced the opponent to lift the shuttlecock.
  2. Qualification Criteria Be able to list two options for returning a serve, along with the subsequent positioning required for each.

Choose a Full BWF Replay to Practice

Class Notes · Practice and Observations

Use three key moments—the serve, the return, and the third shot—to practice understanding the court space and positioning in doubles.

Issues to Be Addressed in This Lesson

When watching doubles matches, if you focus solely on the shuttlecock, it’s easy to overlook how the serve and return have altered the players’ positions. In this lesson, we’ll break down the beginning of a rally into the serve, the return, and the third shot, observing which player achieves a higher hitting position first and which player is forced to step back or lift the shuttlecock. This is a method for learning to read the game; it does not mean there is only one correct way to play every rally.

The First Shot—First, Consider the Limitations and Options

Observe the height and direction of the serve, as well as your opponent’s preparatory stance. A short serve often forces the receiver to make a quick decision at the net, while the server must also be ready to follow up with the next shot. The BWF TV video below features Lin Dan demonstrating his backhand serve technique; it’s a good resource for observing his preparatory movements and shuttle contact. This site uses it as a technical supplement and does not treat a single demonstration as a complete doubles strategy.

The Second Shot—Movement Based on the Landing Spot of the Return

After returning a serve, don’t rush to judge whether it was a good or bad shot. Instead, note where the shuttlecock landed, whether your opponent was forced to move, and whether you were able to transition smoothly into your next shot. Returning the shuttlecock to the backcourt may buy you time to adjust, but it could also give up the initiative; driving it to the net may put pressure on your opponent, but it also requires proper preparation and judgment. Understanding your options through real-life scenarios is more practical than memorizing set answers.

The Third Shot—See How the Two Players Coordinate

The third shot often reveals whether the players have established a front-back or side-by-side division of labor. Observe their racket-holding stance, the distance between them, the open spaces on the court, and their first step after returning the shuttlecock. Positioning changes depending on the shuttlecock’s trajectory and the quality of the shot; it’s not the case that calling “attack” always means front-back positioning, or that calling “defense” always means side-by-side positioning.

Practice Routines for Two Players

Start by limiting the directions of serves and returns; stop after three rallies to discuss. Each player should state one thing: which area they plan to cover and where they hope their partner will return the shuttlecock. Once everyone is comfortable, extend the rallies and gradually introduce different returns. If players repeatedly rush for the shuttlecock or miss it, slow down the pace first and reconfirm their roles.

Notes from the After-Class Session

Choose five rallies and write one sentence for each regarding the direction of the serve, the choice of return, and the positioning for the third shot. When reviewing the replay, verify your observations, note any uncertainties as questions, and then refer to the article on doubles offense and defense rotations on this site. First, explain court positioning and movement, then discuss points won and lost.

After returning a serve down the middle, how do you use the third shot to determine which side has the advantage?

Watch to see if the player hitting the third shot can strike the shuttlecock at a high point in front of them, and observe whether their partner can follow up with a net shot or cover the open space. Then, verify this by seeing if the next shot forces them to lift the shuttlecock.

title: Organizing Your Bag and Maintaining Your Equipment: A Checklist for Before and After Practice
content:
G06 · Beginner · Approx. 20 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Be able to establish a routine for putting away equipment after each shot.

Court Practice

  1. Create a post-game checklist. After your match, separate your wet clothes, shoes, and racket, and once you get home, take out the items that need to air out.
  2. Qualification Criteria Complete the process twice in a row using the checklist; do not mix wet clothes and rackets.

Class Notes · Practice and Observations

Incorporate your shoes, grip, strings, and bag into your regular organization routine to make your next practice go more smoothly.

Check Your Readiness Before Practicing

Before heading out, check your racket, shoes, water, and a change of clothes. If the racket frame has visible cracks or is warped, stop using it immediately and have it inspected by a store; do not continue playing if the strings are broken. If the grip is too wet, the surface is peeling, or you can no longer hold the racket securely, address the issue beforehand to avoid discovering the problem on the court.

Key Points for Checking Your Shoes

Check whether there is dirt on the soles of your shoes, whether the laces are tied securely, and whether the upper and sole are visibly separated. If the court is damp or the soles are in poor condition, address the issue first before starting your activity. When determining whether shoes are suitable, consider how well they support your feet during movement, their lateral stability, and how they feel to you; do not base your decision solely on appearance or brand.

Store Equipment Separately After Practice

After your workout, separate your wet clothes, towels, and shoes from the other items in your racket bag. When you get home, open the bag and let your gear dry in a well-ventilated area, then clean it according to the product instructions. Do not leave wet items sealed inside the bag for long periods, and avoid leaving your racket and shoes in a car exposed to high temperatures.

Daily Log of Grip and String Tension

Keep track of when you change the grip and restring your racket, as well as how the racket feels after use. To determine whether the grip needs replacing, check its sweat-absorbing ability, grip, and how securely it’s attached; for the strings, pay attention to wear and any changes in the feel of your shots. Since usage frequency and playing conditions vary greatly, there’s no single replacement schedule that works for everyone.

Wrapping Up in Two Minutes

We recommend that before leaving the court each time, you wipe down your equipment, sort it, and double-check that nothing is missing, then let it air out at home. Making maintenance a regular routine is easier to stick with than doing a major cleanup once in a while. If you share equipment with other players, be sure to check the size and condition first, clean it after use, and return it to its original place.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can You Use a Hair Dryer to Dry Them? Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions; generally, opt for air drying first and avoid exposing them to direct high heat. Does a brand-new sole guarantee safety? You should still check the condition of the material, the court surface, and the actual grip. For more information, read our articles on selecting and caring for badminton shoes.

title: A Practical Guide to Choosing a Racket: Finding the Right Setup Through Three Rounds of Test Play
content:
G03 · Advanced · Approx. 30 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

You can use a three-round consistency test to compare two rackets.

Court Practice

  1. Start by hitting the shuttlecock from a stationary position, then move around the court to return the shuttlecock, and finally play 5 consecutive rallies. Both players should use the same shuttlecock and the same feeding speed.
  2. Qualification Criteria Compare the results from the three rounds and clearly identify the factor that most influenced performance.

Class Notes · Rackets and Strings

Compare shuttle control, reaction time, and fatigue levels using consistent shot patterns, and use your test-hit records as a basis for your decision.

Start by Writing Down Your Racket Requirements

Before choosing a racket, make a list of whether you primarily play singles or doubles, how often you play each week, your budget, and the issues that currently trouble you the most. For example, slow reaction times on flat drives, difficulty reaching the backcourt with high clears, or fatigue after prolonged practice. Clearly defining your needs is the only way to determine if a new racket will be helpful—don’t base your decision solely on appearance, which professional players use it, or price.

Round 1—Comparing Control

With similar string tension and grip settings, start by practicing serves, net shots, and targeted clear shots—which are easy to repeat. Observe whether the racket face is easy to control and whether the shuttle’s direction matches your expectations. If there is a significant difference in string tension between the two rackets, make a note of this discrepancy to avoid attributing all your sensations to the racket frame.

Round 2—Comparing Reaction and Transition

Incorporate flat drives, return serves, and continuous swings, and observe whether the transition from the previous stroke back to the ready position is smooth. Weight, balance, shaft response, and grip thickness all influence how the racket feels, so a single specification cannot fully determine its suitability. Start by testing at a moderate speed; there’s no need to hit smashes at full power right from the start.

Round 3—Comparing the Feel of Playing Continuously

Feeling powerful for a short time is different from being able to maintain your form throughout an entire match. After trying out a racket, note whether you’re gripping it too tightly, if your swing rhythm is disrupted, and whether you can maintain consistent control of the shuttlecock when fatigued. If you experience discomfort, stop and review your form and the physical strain—don’t treat enduring pain as a necessary part of the racket-selection process.

Keeping a Simple Record of Your Practice Sessions

For each racket, use a five-point scale to rate control, responsiveness, and comfort, then add a line with specific examples—such as whether it’s easier to lift the racket when returning serves, or if you clearly can’t keep up during consecutive rallies. This is a personal comparison tool, not an objective performance ranking. Using the same set of test shots makes comparisons easier than hitting just one or two different shots.

Adjust the String Pattern Next

First, get a feel for the racket itself, then gradually adjust the strings and grip. If you change too many settings at once, it’s hard to tell which one is making a difference. For more information, check out our guides on racket basics and string tension on this site, and be sure to follow the usage limits specified on your equipment.

When hitting from a stationary position, I prefer Racket A, but when moving and returning the shuttlecock, Racket B feels more stable. How should I keep track of this?

Record the results of three separate rounds—static shots, movement, and continuous play—separately, then select the priority based on the game situations you typically encounter. Retest under the same conditions if necessary.

title: backhand low serve Lesson: Establishing the First Three Strokes Through Placement and Rhythm
content:
B05 · Beginner · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Able to place a backhand drop shot near the front service line.

Court Practice

  1. Serve 10 shuttles to each side of the court, aiming for the area behind the short service line. Record your wind-up for the first 3 shuttles and the last 3 shuttles.
  2. Qualification Criteria Land at least 6 shots on each side within the target area, and be ready for the third shot immediately after hitting the shuttlecock.

Class Notes · Serves and Return of Serves

From a Consistent Ready Position to a 10-Shot Streak—Develop a Stable Backhand Drop Shot and Transition to the Next Shot.

Lesson Objectives

When practicing the backhand drop shot, don’t just focus on whether the shuttlecock clears the net—also pay attention to its height, landing spot, and whether your follow-through is consistent. In this lesson, we’ll start with drills targeting specific landing spots before introducing a receiver. Aim for consistency first, and avoid compensating for an unfamiliar feel at contact by suddenly accelerating or making a sudden, forceful swing.

Key Points for Preparation and shuttle Contact

Assume a stance that allows you to maintain your balance, hold the racket in front of you, and grip the handle using the thumb grip suitable for a backhand serve. Stay relaxed during the preparatory phase, keep your swing compact, and ensure that the position of the racket head relative to the racket face is easy to replicate. After striking the shuttlecock, return the racket to a position ready for the next shot. Observe the technical details in the BWF Development instructional materials below. The legality of serves in official matches should be determined according to the applicable rules.

Ten-Shuttlecock Placement Drill

Place a safe, flat visual marker in front of the diagonal service box; avoid using objects that could cause you to trip. Serve ten consecutive shuttles, recording the number of times each shuttle clears the net, lands in the legal service box, and approaches the target area. If the shuttle frequently goes into the net, first check your racket face and the direction of the shot; if it frequently goes too high, reduce the swing amplitude and re-establish your feel for the shuttle. Adjust only one variable at a time.

Connecting the Serve to the Next Shot

Ask your partner to return the shuttlecock in only one direction at first, so you can complete your preparation and take your first step after serving. Then gradually introduce returns in other directions. This will help you check whether you relax immediately after serving or focus only on the landing spot and forget to prepare your grip. Alternate between serving and receiving drills, and exchange observations at the end of each set.

What to Look for When Watching Videos

First, observe the position of the racket and shuttlecock as the demonstrator prepares. Then, watch how the racket returns to the ready position after a short-range push and stroke. The text on this site provides practice guidelines and viewing tips; it is not a word-for-word translation of the video. You can pause the video to compare it with your own movements, so you don’t just play it continuously without paying attention to the key points.

Self-Assessment After Class

Compare the records of the two sets of ten shots—one before and one after—and observe whether the shots are landing in a more concentrated area, rather than just picking out the best shot. Once your form is consistent, increase the pressure on the receiver; if your form changes significantly as a result, lower the difficulty first. For further reading, check out our article on doubles serve and return positioning.

My short serve success rate is already 60 percent—what variations should I try next?

First, have the player hit the shuttlecock to the same spot consistently and return to the ready position after each serve. Then, have your partner return the first shot. The goal for the next round is to be able to return the third shot.

title: Net-Play Step-In Lesson: First, Plant Your Feet Firmly; Then, Hit the Shuttlecock Over the Net
content:
B02 · Beginner · Approx. 25 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

Maintaining balance and returning to your position after hitting a shot at the net.

Court Practice

  1. Practice 6 slow shots on each side of the net. After hitting each shot, pause briefly to check your balance, then slowly connect your footwork.
  2. Qualification Criteria Out of 12 shots, at least 8 should be hit without needing to take a step to regain balance afterward.

Class Notes · Footwork and Movement

Link your start, movement, stride, and return to position, and use stationary drills to develop balanced net play.

Lesson Objectives

This lesson focuses on maintaining control of your body and racket angle while moving to and from the net. Start by simply hitting the shuttlecock over the net, then work on aiming for specific landing spots, and finally increase your speed. Before practicing, make sure the court is dry, your shoe soles are clean, and there is sufficient space to your left, right, and behind you. The following is a self-practice routine; if you feel any discomfort while taking steps, reduce the range of motion and stop forcing yourself to stretch.

Breaking Down the Movement into Four Key Points

Start from a natural ready position. When your opponent hits the shuttlecock, make a small initial move, and only start moving after you’ve assessed the shuttlecock’s trajectory. When approaching the net, take your final step with your racket-side foot, extend your arm toward the shuttlecock, and keep your torso stable. Do not lunge forward with your entire head and upper body just to reach the shuttlecock; after hitting the shuttlecock, regain your balance first, then use appropriate footwork to return to a position ready to handle the next shot. Left-handed players should reverse the left and right directions.

Stage 1—Stationary and Off-shuttle Lunge Steps

Start without a shuttlecock. Stand in a position where you can comfortably take a step forward, and perform a sequence of movements consisting of a step forward, a brief pause, and returning to your starting position. Do six repetitions per set, practicing separately on the left and right sides, with a rest between sets. Observe whether your landing is smooth, whether the direction of your toes and knees is coordinated, and whether you need to sway excessively when returning to your starting position. If you’re barely making it to the target each time by taking large strides, first shorten the distance between your starting point and the target.

Phase 2—Incorporating Hand Tosses

Ask a partner to toss the shuttlecock to a fixed spot that’s easy to reach, and practice hitting the shuttlecock in front of you and sending it over the net. Play in sets of ten shuttles, and record the number of times you can balance your stride and return to your position; this is the recording method recommended by this site and is not an official skill rating. Only after you’ve stabilized your technique should you slightly alter the landing spot—do not increase speed, distance, and unpredictability all at once.

Common Problems and Corrections

If you can’t get back into position after the shuttlecock has crossed the net, first check whether you started your movement too late or took an extra step before hitting the shuttlecock. If the shuttlecock frequently flies too high, reduce unnecessary racket swing and practice fine-tuning your racket face control. The goal of practice is to achieve consistent balance and placement; there’s no need to imitate the extreme reach of professional players.

After-Class Practice and Further Study

Use your phone to record a sequence of movements from the side to check whether the final step, point of contact, and return to position flow smoothly. Focus on adjusting only one aspect at a time. You can return to the “Footwork and Movement” section to read the article on the starting step, and then refer to the net play and stride exercises in the BWF Shuttle Time instructional materials.

Self-Assessment

After hitting the shuttlecock at the net, you need to take another step forward to steady yourself. How can you practice this?

Start by shortening the distance from which the shuttlecock is served, and begin by taking slow steps to return the shuttlecock. Once you can stop yourself upon landing and get ready to return to your position, gradually increase the serving distance.

title: An Effective Badminton Practice Session: A Plan from Warm-up to Cool-down, Including Multi-Shuttlecock Drills
content:
B04 · Beginner · Approx. 30 minutes

What You'll Learn in This Lesson

The ability to organize practice sessions into a repeatable routine.

Court Practice

  1. Schedule a 5-minute warm-up, 15 minutes of a single skill, and a 5-minute follow-up assessment. Write down today’s sole practice goal and the number of times you succeeded.
  2. Qualification Criteria Be able to repeat the test in the same way during your next practice session and explain one movement that needs adjustment.

First, Understand This Topic

When practice time is limited, start by deciding what you want to improve today—for example, return speed, backhand lifts, or serve placement. The more specific your focus, the easier it is to tell whether your practice is helping. Before you begin, warm up with light jogging, shoulder, elbow, and wrist exercises, and dynamic hip, knee, and ankle stretches. Then, get into the groove with low-intensity racket swings and short-distance movements. Don’t go all out with smashes as soon as you step onto the court; let your body gradually adjust to the pace.

Practice and Selection Methods

The main training routine can progress from simple to complex: Start by hitting multiple shuttles from a fixed position to master the movement patterns, then introduce variations in two directions, and finally integrate movement, decision-making, and shot-returning. Keep each set at a pace that allows you to maintain the quality of your movements, and take breaks between sets to rehydrate. If, toward the end of a set, you find yourself merely chasing the shuttlecock and losing your balance while swinging the racket, slow down or end the set—don’t force yourself to complete the planned number of repetitions.

Note a Detail You Can Adjust

At the end of your session, walk slowly to cool down and do some gentle stretches, then record the date, topic, number of sets, and how your body feels. Briefly note one movement that felt most stable and one area that needs adjustment, so you can build on it or lower the difficulty next time. Your training plan doesn’t have to be complicated—the key is to have a clear starting point, make it repeatable, and know when to stop when you’re tired. Movement drills can be combined with A Special Feature on Footwork and Movement Gradually Increase Variety.
